html:
The Battle of Bouvines was fought on 27 July 1214 at Bouvines, near Lille in the north of today's France. King Philip II of France beat an allied army led by the German emperor Otto IV.

Ten years earlier Philip had taken Normandy, Anjou and most of the other French lands of King John of England. To win them back, John paid for a coalition with his nephew Otto and the counts of Flanders and Boulogne. The plan was to attack from two sides: John from the southwest, the allies from the north. John's part failed early in July. Philip then turned north and met the allies at the bridge of Bouvines. He had about 7,000 men and the allies somewhat more, though estimates vary. In the centre Philip was pulled from his horse by Flemish foot soldiers and saved by his knights. The French cavalry won on both wings, Otto fled, and the counts were taken prisoner.

Philip kept his conquests, and the French crown became the strongest power in western Europe. The Angevin Empire was finished, and Otto lost his throne. John went home beaten, and within a year his barons forced him to accept Magna Carta.
